Before you leave

Save your spreadsheet separately and submit it in Canvas. Guide progress stays in this browser and may not follow you to another computer. Keep important calculations in your notebook or spreadsheet. This guide does not submit work or write to Excel.

01 / Set up

You are the estimator.

Your job is to decide what to buy, how much to buy, and what it costs. Your finished product is the completed estimate spreadsheet, supported by your counts and calculations.

Start in Canvas: download the Building Materials Cost Estimate spreadsheet from the Canvas assignment. Open the framing drawing there if you need the full sheet; enlarged elevations are also included below.
  1. Download the spreadsheet from Canvas and save your own copy. Include your name in the filename.
  2. Have your completed Concrete Pad Estimate available.
  3. Use Sheet1. Enter purchase quantities in column E and unit prices in column F. Column G calculates each cost; G39 totals the estimate.
  4. Keep a count or calculation for every quantity. Use the work-log boxes in this guide or your notebook.
Quantity purchased × price per purchase unit = item cost

A quantity means the unit in column D: boards, sheets, gallons, rolls, or squares. It does not always mean square feet.

Use these classroom assumptions
  • One common shed: use the supplied drawing for framing and opening counts. Use the teacher’s supplied roof measurements below for roof coverage and trim, and the supplied gable height for wall area. The model screenshots show a different door and orientation; do not count openings from those screenshots.
  • Uninsulated shed: enter 0 in E15 (interior OSB), E17 (wall insulation), and E29 (roof insulation). Omit interior partition walls.
  • Fixed classroom prices: retain the provided rates. These are practice values, not current store quotes. No shopping or phone calls are required.
  • Door correction: change D21 to “Double door — 5 ft × 80 in.” Keep the $250 classroom allowance for the complete door unit.
  • Rafter correction: change D24 to “2 × 6 — 10 ft.” Keep $2.89 as a classroom price allowance only. An 8-ft board cannot span the supplied roof slope.
  • Rounding: round purchase counts up after calculating the amount needed. Keep measurement decimals until the final step. Use the quantities from your earlier pad estimate as recorded.
  • Scope: estimate the listed materials, with no labor, tax, delivery, or extra percentage for waste. Allow for cutting through the stock-board rules below. This is a classroom estimate, not a construction specification.
02 / Read the shed

A few measurements. Many materials.

Whole roof · both slopes together347.45 ft²Use once for roof coverage.
One eave · two equal eaves18′–9½″18.7917 ft including overhangs
One rake · four sloped gable edges9′–2 15/16″9.2448 ft including overhang
Gable wall height above 8-ft level4′–9 9/16″4.796875 ft, vertically to underside of ridge

The wall footprint is 12 ft × 16 ft; rectangular wall height is 8 ft. The roof pitch is 9:12. Use the supplied measurements rather than trying to measure the drawing on your screen.

How to convert feet and inches

Convert the fractional inch first, then divide all inches by 12.

18′–9½″ = 18 + (9.5 ÷ 12) = 18.7917 ft

Do not enter 18.95 or 18.5. Feet-and-inches notation is not a decimal.

04 / Walls · spreadsheet rows 8–12 and 18

Count the skeleton before the skin.

Work through all four elevations. A visible pair of parallel lines usually represents the edges of one board, not two boards. Double members are separate boards placed together.

Vertical members

Common stud: regular full-height wall member.
King stud: full-height stud beside an opening.
Trimmer: shorter stud supporting a header.
Cripple: short stud above or below an opening, or in a gable.

Horizontal & sloping members

Header: beam over an opening; count both plies.
Sill: horizontal piece under a window.
Sole plate: bottom of wall.
Top plates: double horizontal layer, plus the extra sloped plates at the gable ends.

Count one wall at a time

Choose an elevation below. Enlarge it if needed. On a printed copy, highlight each member as you count it. With the digital drawing, record each wall in the tally table so you do not lose your place.

East elevation · two windows. Orientation follows the supplied drawing.

ElevationFull-height studsShort 2 × 4 pieces*Notes / corner ownership

*Include trimmers, window sills, opening cripples, and gable studs. Exclude plates, headers, and rafters. A full-height king stud belongs only in the full-height column.

Corner rule: assign each physical corner member to one wall. Do not count the same member again just because it is visible in the adjoining elevation. Note your assignments in the table.

Turn the tally into purchase quantities

RowMethod for this estimate
8 · Full studsAdd your four full-height counts. Buy one 92⅝-in. stud for each full-height member.
9 · Partial studsFor this independent-work estimate, reserve one 8-ft 2 × 4 per short piece. This is a deliberately conservative cutting allowance because the drawing does not dimension every short member. Do not add another waste percentage. Record the allowance in your work log.
10 · Top platesStep 1: perimeter = 2(12 + 16) = 56 ft.
Step 2: two horizontal courses = 112 ft; 112 ÷ 8 = 14 boards.
Step 3: add 4 separate boards for the sloped gable plates.
Enter 18 boards in E10. The 14-board result is only the horizontal portion.
11 · Sole platesUse the full 56-ft perimeter before cutting out the doorway. Divide by 8 and round up. This keeps the door cutout as waste.
12 · HeadersThere are 3 openings: 2 windows and 1 double-door opening. Each header has 2 plies. Under our one-board-per-ply allowance, 3 × 2 = 6 boards.
Enter 6 in E12. Two is the ply count for one header, not the total board count. Keep headers out of the partial-stud tally.
18 · Anchor boltsUse a teacher-guide allowance of 12 bolts total for this estimate. The source does not specify a bolt layout; this supplied allowance is not a code-based design.
Why not divide all short lengths by 8?

Stock boards must fit the actual cuts. Three 5-ft pieces total 15 ft, but require three 8-ft boards, not two. A cutting plan must show which pieces fit on each board and allow for the saw cut. Our one-board-per-piece allowance is conservative and makes this task possible with the supplied drawing.

05 / Wall coverings · rows 13–17

From wall area to packages.

Use the same classroom wall dimensions for everyone: four 8-ft-high rectangles plus two triangular gables. For this introductory estimate, use gross wall area without subtracting doors or windows. This is a simple allowance for cuts around openings; do not add an extra waste percentage.

Four wall rectangles

2(16 × 8) + 2(12 × 8)

There are two long walls and two short walls.

Two gable triangles

2 × ½ × 12 × 4.796875

Use vertical height, not the sloped roof edge.

Gross wall area = rectangles + both triangles

CellPurchase unitYour calculation
E13 · Wall sheathing4 × 8 sheet = 32 ft²Gross wall area ÷ 32; round up
E14 · SidingBundle covers 200 ft²Gross wall area ÷ 200; round up
E15 · Interior finishExcludedEnter 0
E16 · PaintGallon covers 400 ft² for one coatGross wall area × 2 coats ÷ 400; round up
E17 · Wall insulationExcludedEnter 0
Worked example with different dimensions

A different shed has 370 ft² of wall area. Its sheathing estimate is 370 ÷ 32 = 11.5625, so buy 12 sheets. For two coats of paint: 370 × 2 ÷ 400 = 1.85, so buy 2 gallons. Use your own wall area for this shed.

06 / Roof · rows 23–31

Area buys coverage. Length buys trim.

347.45 ft² already includes both roof slopes. Do not double it, and do not use the 12 × 16 floor area in its place.

A. Cover the roof

CellPurchase unitMethod
E26 · Sheathing32 ft² per sheet347.45 ÷ 32, rounded up
E27 · Roofing felt500 ft² per roll in this template347.45 ÷ 500, rounded up
E28 · Shingles100 ft² per square347.45 ÷ 100, rounded up to whole squares
E29 · InsulationExcludedEnter 0
Squares and bundles are different units. This spreadsheet prices shingles by the square. One square equals three bundles. Enter whole squares in E28; do not enter the bundle count against a per-square price.

B. Count the roof framing

Use this simplified classroom framing layout: rafter pairs at 16-in. spacing across the 16-ft wall length, including a pair at each end. Double the pair at each gable wall. Overhang support is included only through the blocking allowance below; do not invent additional fly rafters.

  1. Convert the 16-ft length to inches. Divide by 16 to find the number of spaces.
  2. Add one to find the number of rafter-pair positions.
  3. Multiply by two for the two roof slopes.
  4. Add four individual rafters: an extra one on each slope at each of the two gable walls.
CellPurchase method
E23 · Ridge boardUse the 18.7917-ft roof length. Divide by 8 and round up to stock boards. This is a material-length estimate, not a ridge-splice detail.
E24 · RaftersOne 10-ft board per individual rafter. Confirm you changed D24. Use the count from the steps above.
E25 · BlockingUse a classroom allowance of 24 blocks, each 14½ in. long, representing 12 bays on each of two sides. Six blocks fit in one 8-ft board with room for saw cuts.
24 blocks ÷ 6 blocks per board = 4 boards.
Enter 4 in E25. A blank cell produces $0 and leaves this material out of your total.

C. Follow the roof edges

Column E needs purchased pieces, not linear feet. Column F prices one 10-ft board or section. Calculate length first, then convert to pieces before entering the quantity.

Fascia · E30

All perimeter edges: 2 eaves + 4 rakes. The ridge is not part of the perimeter.

1. Find the total length:
2(18.7917) + 4(9.2448) = 74.5626 linear ft.

2. Allocate 10-ft boards:
2 eaves × 2 boards = 4 boards.
4 rakes × 1 board = 4 boards.

Enter 8 boards in E30

3. Check cost: 8 × $12.69 = $101.52.

74.5626 is the length needed, not the number of boards purchased.

Drip edge · E31

Follow the original assignment’s scope: the two eaves only.

1. Find the total length:
2(18.7917) = 37.5834 linear ft.

2. Allocate 10-ft sections:
2 eaves × 2 sections = 4 sections.

Enter 4 sections in E31

3. Check cost: 4 × $3.79 = $15.16.

37.5834 is the length needed, not the number of sections purchased. This classroom scope omits gable-edge drip trim.

Why use a cutting allocation?

Adding lengths and dividing by stock length is only a first check. Separate edges must still be covered by usable pieces. Here, two 10-ft pieces cover each 18.7917-ft eave, and one covers each 9.2448-ft rake. The quantities fit the individual edges.

08 / Check & submit

Make the estimate reviewable.

The spreadsheet is your estimate. This guide’s work log supports it; it is not a substitute for the completed workbook.

  • Every required quantity has a source, count, or calculation.
  • Purchase counts are whole numbers; concrete follows the earlier pad estimate.
  • Check E10 = 18 top-plate boards, E12 = 6 header boards, and E25 = 4 blocking boards under this guide’s allowances.
  • Check E30 = 8 fascia boards and E31 = 4 drip-edge sections. Do not enter linear footage in those cells.
  • E15, E17, and E29 are explicitly 0.
  • The corrected door and rafter descriptions are saved.
  • G3:G38 calculate quantity × unit cost, and G39 totals all item costs.
  • Floor, walls, openings, and roof are all included before calling the total final.
If a spreadsheet total is not working

Click an item-cost cell. For row 8, its formula should be =E8*F8. The total in G39 should be =SUM(G3:G38). Enter numbers without unit text in E and F. A blank quantity can silently contribute zero, so check for missing entries even when the total looks reasonable.

Before submitting: save your completed spreadsheet, return to the Canvas assignment, and upload it there. Include the work log only if your teacher requests it. This tutorial has no upload or submission controls.
